prompt.context: Your client is an international chain of fitness centers operating in Sub-Saharan Africa, Europe and Southeast Asia. GymCo missed its 2019 growth target of ZAR600M. The CEO would like you to investigate what is going on.
prompt.question: GymCo has missed its revenue growth target. What is going on, and what should GymCo do about it?

clarifying_info.a: There are 2 major gym chains. GymCo has 60% market share, FitnessCo has 30%, and a few small chains the remaining 10%.
GymCo members pay a monthly membership fee of approximately ZAR700 per month.
Market trends are in favour of gyms — consumers are switching to healthier habits.
A few smaller competitors have recently entered the market — smaller gyms offering more classes with less focus on free weights and cardio.

clarifying_info.q: Are competitors also experiencing revenue declines?
clarifying_info.a: No other competitors have noticed any decline in revenues; in fact, they have had strong increases over the past 12 months.

exhibits.title: Revenue and Number of Members Over Time
exhibits.shows: A dual-axis chart tracking total number of members (in thousands) and total revenue (ZAR millions) month by month across 2012 and 2013, alongside monthly new member additions and churn rates.

data.members_trend: Ranges from approximately 350K to 489K across the period shown
data.revenue_trend: Ranges from approximately 426M to 476M, with revenue growth appearing to plateau or decline relative to member growth

framework: Revenue = Number of Members x Revenue per Member
Number of Members = Existing Members - Churn + New Members
Revenue per Member = Initial quoted price - Signing discount / promotional adjustments
Investigate why revenue per member is declining even as total member count grows
Identify the root cause of the unusual churn and re-join spike in early 2013

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1. What do you observe, and what hypothesis does it suggest?
questions.guidance: Strong candidate notices: (1) member count is increasing but revenue growth is lagging, so revenue per member must be falling; (2) there is a dramatic one-month spike in both churn (30%) and new sign-ups (205K) in the same period that revenue starts declining; (3) this pattern suggests members left and rejoined — possibly to take advantage of a discount or promotion. Candidate should want to explore whether a discount scheme was introduced.

questions.prompt: After the exhibit analysis: GymCo partnered with a large health insurer (HealthCo) in 2012, offering 40% off (ZAR400 pm instead of ZAR700 pm) to HealthCo members. During 2013, management noticed members were leaving, switching health insurers to HealthCo, and rejoining at the discounted rate. Roughly 50% of people who left in 2013 rejoined at the lower rate. How should we assess the financial impact of this HealthCo contract?
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the incremental financial impact into: (1) Additional revenues from brand-new members who joined solely because of the discount; (2) Foregone revenues from existing members who switched to the HealthCo discount (would have paid ZAR700 but now pay ZAR400); (3) Foregone revenues from new members who would have joined at full price regardless of the discount.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the net financial impact of the HealthCo contract in 2013.
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify three groups among the 475K new HealthCo discount members, calculate lost and gained revenue for each, and sum to a net figure. A strong answer arrives at approximately ZAR-555M net impact and articulates clearly why the contract is harmful.

math.setup: Segment 475K new HealthCo members into Group 1 (existing members who rejoined), Group 2 (would-have-joined-anyway new members), Group 3 (truly incremental new members). Revenue foregone = discount gap (ZAR300 pm) x count x months. Revenue gained = ZAR400 pm x Group 3 count x months.
steps: Group 1: Existing members who rejoined = 200K (given). All rejoined at start of year so 12 months of discount exposure. Revenue foregone = 200K x (700-400) x 12 = 200K x 300 x 12 = ZAR720M foregone.

Group 2: Brand-new HealthCo sign-ups = 475K total - 200K existing re-joiners = 275K truly new. Of these, 30% would have joined at full price anyway = 275K x 30% = 82.5K. Average membership duration = 6 months (assume joining evenly throughout year). Revenue foregone = 82.5K x (700-400) x 6 = 82.5K x 300 x 6 = ZAR148.5M foregone. (Note: casebook states ZAR297M — this uses the full 82.5K x 300 x 12 interpretation; accept either with consistent assumption.)
Group 3: Truly incremental new members = 275K - 82.5K = 192.5K. Average duration = 6 months. Additional revenue = 192.5K x 400 x 6 = ZAR462M gained.
Net impact = ZAR462M gained - ZAR720M (Group 1) - ZAR297M (Group 2, per casebook using 6-month avg x 2 = full year equivalent or 82.5K x 300 x 12 = ZAR297M) = ZAR462M - ZAR1,017M = -ZAR555M.
Conclusion: The HealthCo contract cost GymCo approximately ZAR555M in net revenue in 2013 — it is deeply detrimental.
math.answer: Net negative financial impact of approximately ZAR555M in 2013.

questions.prompt: What options does GymCo have regarding the HealthCo contract?
questions.guidance: Candidate should evaluate at least 3-4 options with benefits and drawbacks: (1) Exit the deal entirely; (2) Reduce the discount offered; (3) Change rejoining policy (e.g., no re-joining within 12 months of leaving); (4) Convert discount to a limited-term offer (e.g., discounted only for first 6 months). Strong answer notes the trade-off between retaining new-member pipeline vs. protecting revenue per existing member.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategies could GymCo use to grow its member base organically, without relying on the HealthCo partnership?

categories.name: Pricing & Promotions
ideas: Offer discounts for annual upfront subscriptions
Referral bonuses for existing members who bring in friends
Corporate wellness partnerships at full or near-full rates

categories.name: Product & Service
ideas: Add more group fitness classes to compete with boutique gyms
Introduce premium tiers (personal training bundles, nutrition coaching)
Upgrade equipment and facilities to justify premium pricing
Launch a digital/app-based offering for at-home workouts

categories.name: Marketing & Brand
ideas: Targeted social media and influencer campaigns
Community fitness events to raise brand visibility
Seasonal campaigns tied to New Year, summer body goals, etc.

categories.name: Retention
ideas: Exit surveys and win-back campaigns for churned members
Member engagement tracking to intervene before cancellation
Improved customer service and on-boarding experience

recommendation: GymCo is currently in a detrimental contract with HealthCo that cost the company approximately ZAR555M in net revenue in 2013 — it should seek to cancel or fundamentally renegotiate this agreement.
The contract also creates dangerous over-reliance on HealthCo for new member acquisition and hands HealthCo significant leverage over GymCo's business model.
GymCo should develop an organic growth strategy to replace the member pipeline currently dependent on the HealthCo discount.
risks: Cancelling the contract may cause existing HealthCo-discounted members (409K at year-end) to leave, creating a near-term revenue and membership cliff.
Reducing the discount without a transition plan may trigger member backlash and negative press.
Smaller boutique gym competitors are growing — GymCo must address product differentiation, not just pricing.
next_steps: Quantify the cost-benefit of each contract exit option (full cancellation vs. discount reduction vs. rejoining policy change vs. time-limited discount).
Develop a retention plan for current HealthCo-discount members to migrate them to a full or near-full price tier.
Design and budget an organic member acquisition campaign (referral scheme, corporate wellness, seasonal promotions).
Monitor competitor moves, particularly boutique gym entrants, and assess whether GymCo's class offerings need expansion.
